name: Pyrefly
summary: Meta’s Python type checker and language server, written in Rust, built to replace Pyre and fast enough to re-check code on every save.
intro: Pyrefly checks Python against the typing specification and infers types for unannotated locals and return values, which its editor extension can show and insert. It is written in Rust and designed to serve both batch runs in CI and latency-sensitive editor requests from one engine, so the command line and the IDE agree. Meta says it checks over 1.85 million lines of code per second, type-checks PyTorch 15 times faster than mypy and Pyright, and usually re-checks within 10 milliseconds of saving a file. It has built-in support for Pydantic, Django and pytest; for Pydantic it mirrors runtime validation, so `Order(id="2")` passes where Pyright reports a type error. Settings live in `pyrefly.toml` or `[tool.pyrefly]`; `pyrefly init` migrates a mypy or Pyright configuration, `pyrefly suppress` silences existing errors with comments, and `pyrefly infer` writes annotations.

Version 1.0 (May 2026) declared it stable and added presets (`off`, `basic`, `legacy`, `default`, `strict`, `all`). A project with no Pyrefly configuration to read or migrate gets `basic`, which reports only high-confidence errors such as syntax errors and missing imports. Pyrefly is the default type checker for Instagram’s 20-million-line codebase and has been adopted by PyTorch and JAX. New minor versions ship monthly, and any of them may add new errors, since it does not follow strict semantic versioning.
strengths: Speed on large codebases: Meta reports 1.85 million lines per second and sub-10 ms re-checks in the editor
One engine for CLI and language server, proven on Instagram’s 20-million-line codebase
Framework awareness for Pydantic, Django and pytest out of the box
Migration tools: `pyrefly init` reads mypy or Pyright settings, `pyrefly suppress` and `pyrefly infer` ease adoption
limits: Young: alpha in 2025 and stable only since May 2026, and any monthly release may introduce new type errors
Unconfigured projects get the lenient `basic` preset, which can report nothing on real type errors until you add `[tool.pyrefly]` or pick a preset
Its speed figures come from Meta’s own benchmarks; Astral’s ty claims to be faster still in the editor
Where the typing spec is silent it makes different choices from Pyright and mypy (looser attribute narrowing, Pydantic coercion), so switching checkers changes results

story: In 2017 Meta began building Pyre to type-check Instagram’s huge Python codebase. It was written in OCaml, borrowed its multi-process architecture from Meta’s Hack and Flow checkers, and was designed as a CI and command-line tool that maximised throughput. That fitted the editor badly: computing more than the user needed could freeze the IDE, and Meta temporarily used Pyright as its language server, which brought mismatched errors between the editor and CI.

Meta’s Python language tooling team started over in Rust, developing in the open on GitHub, and announced Pyrefly as an alpha in spring 2025. It reached beta in November 2025 (0.42.0), by which point it was the default language server and type checker for everyone working on Instagram, and stable 1.0 in May 2026.

The rewrite deliberately reversed several Pyre decisions: one engine for both throughput and latency, a parser that recovers from errors, minimal rewriting of the syntax tree so editor features keep exact positions, and friendlier type narrowing on attributes even where that is less strictly sound.

choices.why: Pyre’s OCaml multiprocessing forced shared data into string-to-string tables and struggled on Windows; Rust gave real threads, Windows, macOS and Linux as equals, and a larger contributor pool.

choices.choice: Design for the IDE from the start
choices.why: Pyre was built for throughput in CI and couldn’t be retrofitted for editor latency; Pyrefly was designed to serve both, so the CLI and the editor share one view of the code.

choices.choice: Keep the syntax tree close to the source
choices.why: Pyre lowered many constructs into others, which lost information that find-references and refactoring need; Pyrefly avoids that.

Pyre refused to trust `isinstance` checks on attributes once another function had been called, one of its most frequent complaints; Pyrefly allows that narrowing, trading some soundness for fewer false alarms.
